title: Why distributed systems are hard
subtitle: Once your system runs on two or more machines, parts fail on their own, messages get lost and clocks disagree. Learn what changes and where each problem is solved.

c.v: January 4th, 2021 was the first working day of the year for many people. Slack's traffic jumped. Client
were cold, so apps pulled down more data than usual on their first connection.
Slack's networks on AWS were linked by Transit Gateways. Under the new load, these gateways did not scale fast enough. Part of the network "had indeed become saturated and was dropping
The problem was in the network between the servers. Many calls between them were slow or lost. At 6:57 AM PST, about 99% of messages were sent. On a normal day the rate is above 99.999%.
Then the tools for seeing the problem broke too. The dashboards and alerts ran in a different network from their databases. So they also needed the broken gateways, and they failed.
The machines also read the signs wrong. Threads spent more time waiting on the network, so CPU use dropped.
saw low CPU and removed servers. Later, as waiting threads piled up, the team tried to add 1,200 servers between 7:01 and 7:15 AM. That hit other limits.
also failed at a very high rate. The
have a "panic mode" for this: they spread requests across all servers anyway. That, with
No single machine broke. Some parts worked, some failed, and the automatic tools read the signs wrong. AWS raised the gateway capacity by hand, and the network was normal again by 10:40 AM PST.
This is what distributed systems feel like.

A system is distributed when it runs on more than one machine and the machines talk over a network. Your app server and its database on another host already count. So does a phone app that calls your API.
On one computer, if a part fails, you usually expect the whole computer to stop. In a distributed system, one node can crash while the others keep working. Kleppmann calls this a
Faults in the network or a node can happen at any moment, with no warning.
Partial failure comes with other hard problems:
The network can lose, delay, duplicate or reorder messages.
A caller cannot tell a slow server from a dead one.
There is no shared clock that all machines agree on.
In a distributed system, "I got no answer" does not mean "it did not happen". Design every call so that the caller can live with not knowing.
One call, many places to fail

Gabrielson, from AWS, splits one request and reply into eight steps. The client sends the request, the network delivers it, the server checks it and updates its state. Then the same happens in reverse for the reply.
Any of the eight steps can fail. The client, the server and the network fail independently of each other.
Step through what the caller sees when no reply comes. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
When the client times out, the result is UNKNOWN: the work "may or may not have happened".
Kleppmann gives the classic example. If a client resends a request after no reply, the server may do it twice, such as charging a credit card twice.
Messages can be lost, delayed, duplicated and reordered.
retries lost packets and removes duplicates for you. But TCP usually gives up after a
, typically about a minute. If a
lasts longer, your code needs its own retries and duplicate checks.
Delays can be huge. Kleppmann notes documented cases where packets inside one data center were delayed for more than a minute.
You cannot tell slow from dead
The usual way to spot a dead server is a timeout: send a message and wait for a reply. But silence can also mean that the message was lost or delayed.
The server may also be paused. Stop-the-world
in languages such as Java can pause all threads, and on large heaps the pause can last several minutes.

So a timeout is a guess. Too short, and you mark healthy servers as dead. Too long, and users wait on a server that is gone. In Slack's outage, low CPU looked like low load, but it really meant threads were waiting on the network.
Each machine has its own clock, usually a quartz crystal. Some run a bit fast and some a bit slow, and their speed changes with temperature.
Machines sync their clocks over the network, but the network adds its own error.
So two machines can disagree on "now", and timestamps from different machines may not show the true order of events.
These problems are old. According to Rotem-Gal-Oz, Peter Deutsch, then a Sun fellow, wrote down seven false assumptions in 1994. James Gosling added an eighth in 1997.

Each one feels true on your laptop. Each one is false in production. For the first one, Rotem-Gal-Oz says you must plan for lost calls: retry, acknowledge important messages, and ignore duplicates or make messages
This lesson is a map. Each problem has its own lesson:
When a call gets no reply, you must choose what to do. Each choice has a cost.

c.v: In design reviews, point at each arrow between two boxes and ask:
"What happens if this call is lost, slow or done twice?"
Check that every network call has a timeout you chose on purpose. Do not trust the client library's default; look it up.
Treat a timeout as "unknown", not "failed". Log it as unknown, and
later if money or stock is involved.
Keep monitoring away from the thing it monitors. Slack's dashboards failed because they needed the same broken network.
Be careful with automatic actions based on one signal, such as CPU. A stuck system can look idle.
Test failure, not just success. Gabrielson writes that engineers must assume each step of a call could fail.
He also warns that distributed bugs often show up long after they are deployed.
When you add a new service, list which of the
"List every network call in this code path. For each one, show the timeout, the retry rule, and whether the call is safe to repeat. Mark any call with no timeout."
"This handler calls the payment service and then saves the order. Walk through what happens if the payment call times out but the payment really worked."
"Write a test that makes the stock service reply after 5 seconds, and one where the reply is lost after the work is done. Show what our code does in each case."
The agent did not treat a timeout as "the call failed". Look for code that undoes work it is not sure about.
Retries reuse the same request ID or
. They do not make a new one each time.
Timeouts are set in the real client config, not only in comments or docs.
No logic compares timestamps from two different machines to decide which event came first.
Tests cover a lost reply, not just a lost request. A lost reply is the case where the work was really done.

q.v: Your service calls another service and gets no reply within the timeout. What do you know?

options.v: The request was lost on the network.
Nothing for sure. The request may or may not have been done.

why.v: The request could be lost, the server could be dead or slow, or the reply could be lost. From the caller's side these look the same.

options.v: Some parts of the system fail while other parts keep working.
A server that returns only half of a response.
A failure that fixes itself after a restart.

why.v: On one computer, a fault usually stops everything. In a distributed system, one node or link can fail while the rest keep running.

q.v: Why is it risky to retry a "charge card" call that timed out?

options.v: Retries are always slower than the first call.
The first call may have worked, so a retry can charge the card twice.
The network does not allow the same message twice.

why.v: A timeout means the result is unknown. Make the call safe to repeat, for example with an idempotency key.

q.v: In Slack's January 2021 outage, why did autoscaling first remove servers?

options.v: An engineer turned autoscaling off by mistake.
Threads were waiting on the slow network, so CPU use dropped and looked like low load.
The cloud provider removed the servers to save money.

why.v: The postmortem says waiting threads lowered CPU use, which first started some automatic downscaling.

q.v: Which of these is one of the eight fallacies of distributed computing?

why.v: "The network is reliable" is the first fallacy. The others include "latency is zero" and "bandwidth is infinite".
